title: Baby Shower

jokes.text: Jan simulating labor contractions while Michael coaches her like a birth partner, but they are practicing with a watermelon
jokes.setup: Michael is on the phone with someone describing labor symptoms — 'contractions every 10 minutes,' 'cervix is ripening' — and responding earnestly with coaching advice
jokes.punchline: The narrator reveals Jan is about to have a baby with a sperm donor and Michael is preparing for the birth of a watermelon with Dwight
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed cold open misdirect. The audience assumes Michael is coaching Jan through real labor; the reveal that he is practicing with a watermelon is absurd yet completely in character. The parallel structure (real birth / fake birth) is sophisticated comedy writing. Scores high because the concept is original, the structure is airtight, and it could only be Michael and Dwight.

jokes.text: Jan tells Michael her cervix is ripening; Michael says 'Okay, good' as if receiving a routine status update
jokes.setup: Jan is describing graphic biological details of impending labor to Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael responds with breezy, managerial 'Okay, good' — completely unbothered and treating it like a project milestone
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Michael's calm, affirmative 'Okay, good' to 'my cervix is ripening' is peak character comedy — he's performing competence in a domain he doesn't understand at all. The economy is excellent; the punchline is purely in the delivery and tone mismatch.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'Now this baby will be related to Michael through... Delusion.'
jokes.setup: The narrator sets up a logical question about the baby's relation to Michael
jokes.punchline: The single word answer: 'Delusion' — delivered as a formal family relation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Maximum economy — a single word does all the work. The structure is near-perfect: the setup mimics a formal genealogical question, making 'Delusion' land like a punch. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific to Michael's psychology, and earns its laugh entirely through wit rather than cheap shortcuts. The pause implied by the ellipsis heightens the delivery.

jokes.text: Michael drills Dwight on the birth route — 'Highways or surface roads?' — while Dwight insists he checked and there are no potholes on Gibson
jokes.setup: Michael is running a birth emergency simulation with Dwight, treating it like a military drill
jokes.punchline: Dwight has actually pre-checked the route for potholes, demonstrating his characteristic over-preparation for a completely hypothetical scenario
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Dwight's literal-minded hyper-competence (actually checking the route for potholes) is perfectly in character. The joke rewards knowledge of the character. Not a standout line but works well as part of the extended simulation sequence.

jokes.text: Michael asks Andy, 'Would you like to have my baby?' and Andy immediately says 'Yes!' before Michael shuts it down
jokes.setup: Michael is in the middle of the birth simulation and needs someone to play Jan
jokes.punchline: Andy's instant, enthusiastic 'Yes!' reveals his desperate need for Michael's approval — and the immediate 'No. Okay, no.' punctuates it
jokes.explanation: The joke is almost entirely carried by Andy's character — his sycophantic eagerness makes the 'Yes!' funny on its own, and the brisk 'No. Okay, no.' from Michael treats it as a reasonable offer briefly entertained. Good economy and strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional: 'Babies are one of my many areas of expertise. Growing up, I performed my own circumcision.'
jokes.setup: Dwight establishes himself as a baby expert in a talking-head confessional
jokes.punchline: He performed his own circumcision — stated with complete matter-of-fact Schrute confidence
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Dwight joke. The escalation from 'areas of expertise' to 'I performed my own circumcision' is shocking yet completely consistent with Dwight's Schrute Farm upbringing mythology. Maximum economy, extremely high quotability, and the deadpan delivery implied by the confessional format makes it land harder. This is exactly the kind of absurd-but-grounded specificity that defines the show's best character comedy. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Michael screams 'Cradle my head!' while Dwight coaches him through the watermelon birth simulation
jokes.setup: Michael is playing the laboring mother in the simulation, lying on the floor
jokes.punchline: 'Cradle my head!' — Michael fully committed to the bit, demanding comfort during fake labor
jokes.explanation: Broad physical comedy from Michael's total commitment to the simulation. Funny in context but not particularly clever — the joke is Michael's earnestness, which is a recurring device. Works better as a visual gag than as written dialogue.

jokes.text: Dwight instructs Michael to secretly mark the baby with a Sharpie so 'no baby snatcher could ever copy' the mark — then butters the watermelon before it shoots out
jokes.setup: Dwight is coaching Michael through the baby-marking protocol for when the baby 'emerges'
jokes.punchline: The watermelon is buttered to simulate the slipperiness of a newborn, and it shoots out dramatically
jokes.explanation: Two layered jokes: (1) Dwight's paranoid anti-baby-snatcher Sharpie protocol is a great absurdist character gag, and (2) the buttered watermelon physical punchline is a well-executed visual callback to the setup. Dwight's explanation — 'Newborns are slippery. Nice touch.' — shows his self-satisfied competence. The physical gag elevates what could have been just a dialogue joke.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'This is going to be the happiest day of my life.'
jokes.setup: Michael is excited about the baby shower for a baby that is not his, with an ex-girlfriend he has a complicated history with
jokes.punchline: The sincerity of the statement — Michael genuinely believes this — is darkly funny given the audience knows the day is unlikely to go well
jokes.explanation: A functional irony beat — Michael's delusional optimism is a well-worn character note. Works as a transition moment but doesn't distinguish itself from the standard 'Michael is oblivious' template.

jokes.text: Michael asks Phyllis if she got the live storks for the baby shower
jokes.setup: Michael arrives at the baby shower setup and checks in with Phyllis on decorations
jokes.punchline: He requested live storks — as in actual birds — for the baby shower, and is genuinely annoyed Phyllis didn't get them
jokes.explanation: Michael's literal interpretation of baby shower theming — actually wanting live storks — is a good absurdist character beat. His genuine frustration ('Damn it, Phyllis') makes it better. The joke efficiently communicates Michael's grandiose and impractical event planning in just a few words.

jokes.text: The M&M bowl is labeled 'Astird' because Michael misspelled 'Astrid' when writing the name down
jokes.setup: Phyllis explains the personalized M&Ms with baby names — boy bowl says 'Chevy,' girl bowl says...
jokes.punchline: 'Astird.' Michael wrote it down wrong, and it was followed anyway — Phyllis confirms: 'Michael wrote down Astird.'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed visual/verbal gag. 'Astird' is funny because it's close enough to the real name to suggest genuine obliviousness, and the deadpan confirmation 'Michael wrote down Astird' doubles the joke. Also foreshadows the running name mispronunciation gag. Good economy.

jokes.text: Talking head reaction to 'Astird' — someone looks pained at the camera
jokes.setup: The M&M name misspelling has just been revealed
jokes.punchline: A deadpan reaction shot to camera — the silent acknowledgment of Michael's incompetence
jokes.explanation: A standard reaction beat — functional but not distinguished. The 'Astird' itself is the better joke; this is a clean button on it.

jokes.text: Michael tells Phyllis 'we all came into this room and gave you a golden shower' — referring to her wedding shower — without realizing what 'golden shower' means
jokes.setup: Michael is upbraiding Phyllis for not doing enough for the baby shower, reminding her that the office threw her a wedding shower
jokes.punchline: 'We all came into this room and gave you a golden shower' / 'Where's my golden shower, Phyllis?' — Michael uses the term with complete innocence
jokes.explanation: A classic Michael Scott double-entendre delivered in complete sincerity. The joke works because Michael's obliviousness is total — he's genuinely complaining about reciprocity. 'Where's my golden shower, Phyllis?' as a righteous demand is highly quotable. This type of accidental vulgarity is a signature Michael Scott gag and this is a good specimen of it. High quotability, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'It does not matter to me at all whether this baby is biologically mine. I'm going to love it. It's like when the dog nurses the tiger cub. Have you seen that video? It is so bizarre and unnatural, but it happens.'
jokes.setup: Michael is earnestly expressing his emotional connection to Jan's baby
jokes.punchline: His chosen metaphor for unconditional love is a dog nursing a tiger cub — which he then describes as 'bizarre and unnatural' without recognizing that undercuts his point
jokes.explanation: An excellent Michael Scott confessional. The joke has two layers: (1) he uses an animal video to explain human love, which is classic Michael, and (2) he undermines his own metaphor by calling it 'bizarre and unnatural' — the self-sabotaging sincerity is the funniest part. This is the kind of layered absurdism that distinguishes great Office writing. Strong character integration — only Michael would pick this metaphor and then immediately question it.

jokes.text: Kevin asks why they have to pay money for 'his ex-girlfriend's unborn sperm-bank baby'
jokes.setup: Phyllis is collecting money for the baby shower gift
jokes.punchline: Kevin's blunt, legally accurate description of the situation — 'his ex-girlfriend's unborn sperm-bank baby' — cuts through the social performance everyone else is maintaining
jokes.explanation: Kevin's blunt literalism works here — his condensed description of the situation is funnier than any elaborate setup because of how efficiently it captures the absurdity. Good economy and character integration, though not a top-tier joke.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'Look at it as if you're paying for the cake, not the baby. Sheet cake.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is questioning why they have to contribute to the gift
jokes.punchline: Phyllis reframes it as paying for the cake — then the non-sequitur clarification 'Sheet cake'
jokes.explanation: The 'Sheet cake' clarification is the joke — unnecessarily specific and very Phyllis. Mild but functional. The reframe itself isn't that funny; the specificity of the cake type does the work.

jokes.text: Phyllis talking head: 'I'm no longer under Angela's heel, and her little grape head is under mine.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis has taken over as head of the Party Planning Committee
jokes.punchline: 'Her little grape head is under mine' — a surprisingly ruthless and petty metaphor from sweet Phyllis
jokes.explanation: The physical specificity of 'grape head' is what makes this great — it's a weirdly precise insult from someone who normally seems passive. The contrast between Phyllis's gentle demeanor and the vindictiveness of the metaphor is the joke. High economy. Quotable.

jokes.text: Angela appears and tells Phyllis not to talk to the camera crew, ordering her to 'Make the party' — implying she's lurking and monitoring Phyllis
jokes.setup: Phyllis is doing a talking head about her new power
jokes.punchline: Angela appears immediately, still policing Phyllis even from a subordinate position — 'Don't talk to them. Make the party, please, Phyllis.'
jokes.explanation: Angela refusing to accept her demotion and still trying to control Phyllis is a good character beat. The joke is the power dynamic — Phyllis just bragged about having Angela under her thumb, and here's Angela still giving orders. The juxtaposition with the previous confessional is the real punchline.

jokes.text: Jim on the phone with Pam while she tells an extremely convoluted art school story — Jim can barely follow the names and keeps getting corrected
jokes.setup: Jim is at the office and Pam calls from art school with an urgent story about Sarikaya, Stacy, Foner, and a light box
jokes.punchline: Jim keeps confusing details, Pam corrects him with increasing exasperation, and the story culminates in Jim not knowing who anyone is — 'No, Stacy is a boy.'
jokes.explanation: The joke is really about the growing distance between Jim and Pam — he doesn't know any of her new friends, she's frustrated he can't keep up with her world. 'Stacy is a boy' is the best beat. Emotionally resonant comedy that does character work, though a bit long to execute.

jokes.text: Pam: 'No, Stacy is a boy.' Jim: 'This is so frustrating. Why can't you just be in art class with me?'
jokes.setup: Jim has been trying to follow Pam's art school story, making assumptions about 'Stacy'
jokes.punchline: Jim's plaintive 'Why can't you just be in art class with me?' — which makes no logical sense but perfectly captures his emotional state
jokes.explanation: A gem of a line — Jim's frustration boils over into an illogical wish ('be in art class WITH me') that is both funny and genuinely touching. The misdirection from 'this is so frustrating' (which you expect to be about the story) to a confession of missing her is well-executed. Character-specific to Jim's way of expressing vulnerability through mild absurdism.

jokes.text: After hanging up, Jim says to no one: 'That was a good story.' Then: 'Who's Sarikaya Komzin?'
jokes.setup: Jim has just gotten off a confusing phone call with Pam about people he doesn't know
jokes.punchline: He tells the camera it was a good story — clearly it wasn't — then immediately proves it by asking who the main character was
jokes.explanation: A clean, efficient button on the phone call sequence. 'That was a good story' is the deadpan Jim-to-camera look equivalent, and 'Who's Sarikaya Komzin?' immediately undercuts it. Two lines, two laughs, excellent economy. Classic Jim talking-head structure.

jokes.text: Andy shows off the baby photo guessing game — 'Who would have thought that this little baby would be marrying that little baby?'
jokes.setup: Andy is enthusiastically presenting the baby photo guessing game at the party
jokes.punchline: His framing implies two baby photos are a romantic couple, which is vaguely creepy and accidental
jokes.explanation: A mild gag — Andy's over-enthusiasm and his odd framing of the baby pictures as a romantic pairing. Functional but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Baby photo game: Andy identifies a baby photo as two babies who would grow up to marry each other, then discovers one is Phyllis
jokes.setup: The office is playing a game matching baby photos to employees; Andy is enthusiastically commenting on two cute babies
jokes.punchline: 'That's Phyllis.' The romantic implication Andy made about two babies suddenly applies to Phyllis as a baby — Andy's compliment retroactively becomes weird
jokes.explanation: Competent structural joke. Andy's romantic observation about two mystery babies becomes retroactively creepy when one is revealed to be Phyllis — 'Pervert.' is earned. Works because the setup is long enough that the reveal lands with force. Not exceptional but well-timed.

jokes.text: The baby photo turns out to be Phyllis. Andy: 'I hope you two are very happy together. Pervert.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been romantically framing two baby photos; someone calls him out
jokes.punchline: One of the photos is Phyllis's baby picture — making Andy's earlier romantic framing inadvertently creepy, and he immediately calls whoever guessed it a 'pervert'
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure — the reveal that one photo is Phyllis retroactively makes Andy's romantic framing weird, and his immediate deflection ('Pervert') is a funny reversal. The irony that he's the one who set up the implication is the joke.

jokes.text: Michael approaches Holly with 'Ahoy, matey!'
jokes.setup: Michael needs to talk to Holly but has promised Jan he'll act cold toward her
jokes.punchline: His opening is 'Ahoy, matey' — his attempt at breezy coolness is bizarre and slightly creepy
jokes.explanation: A quick odd-Michael character beat — the pirate greeting is charming in its weirdness but not a developed joke. Context-dependent.

jokes.text: Michael tells Holly that Jan is 'incredibly fat and enormous right now, extremely unattractive' — then adds that he's treating Ryan the same way
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining to Holly why he'll be acting cold to her while Jan is in the office — framing it as a courtesy to Jan's 'bloated feelings'
jokes.punchline: 'And I'm treating Ryan the same way.' — tacked on casually to make his rudeness seem like a principled policy
jokes.explanation: The Ryan addition is the killer detail — it implies Michael is treating Holly with the same dismissiveness as his nemesis Ryan, which reveals how tangled his feelings are. Well-structured and character-specific. Michael's attempt to be considerate while being deeply inconsiderate is a signature tension.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'I do not like pregnant women in my workspace. They're always complaining. I have varicose veins, too. I have swollen ankles. I'm constantly hungry. Do you think my nipples don't get sore, too?'
jokes.setup: Dwight gives his opinion on pregnant women in the workplace
jokes.punchline: He lists pregnancy symptoms he also experiences — including sore nipples — delivered with complete self-righteous indignation
jokes.explanation: An excellent Dwight confessional. The structure is perfect: he begins with a reasonable-sounding complaint about pregnant women, then pivots to claiming all the same symptoms himself, peaking at 'Do you think my nipples don't get sore, too?' The escalation and Dwight's complete sincerity make this a high-quality joke. The final detail about knowing the fastest route to the hospital connects back to the cold open simulation. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Jan arrives at the office — she has already had the baby, and Michael had no idea
jokes.setup: Michael has been obsessively preparing for Jan's birth all episode
jokes.punchline: Jan walks in holding the baby — she already gave birth without telling Michael
jokes.explanation: A well-earned structural payoff — all of Michael's preparation is revealed to be useless. Jim's 'Oh no.' reaction shot is the punctuation. The joke is situational rather than verbal, and it works because of everything built before it.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'Jan had the baby, and Michael wasn't there to mark it. So the baby could be anybody's, except Michael's.'
jokes.setup: Michael's paranoid Sharpie-marking plan from the simulation
jokes.punchline: The narrator delivers the consequence of missing the birth with perfect deadpan logic: the baby 'could be anybody's, except Michael's'
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback that pays off the Sharpie bit from the cold open. The logic is absurd but internally consistent within Michael's worldview, and the deadpan delivery ('could be anybody's, except Michael's') is perfectly constructed. High economy, strong structure, and the callback earns a bonus because the setup was so well-planted.

jokes.text: Michael calls the baby 'Astird'; Jan corrects him: 'Astrid.' Michael: 'Oh!'
jokes.setup: Michael has been working with the misspelled 'Astird' from the M&Ms
jokes.punchline: He calls the real baby 'Astird' to Jan's face; the correction lands as a small embarrassment
jokes.explanation: A functional running gag payoff — the M&M spelling error paying off when Michael uses the wrong name in person. Mild but satisfying as a callback.

jokes.text: Michael: 'The birth instructor had no sense of humor, and I proved him wrong in so many ways.'
jokes.setup: Jan explains that the birth instructor advised Michael not to be present at the birth
jokes.punchline: Michael's response implies he demonstrated his comedic value to a birth instructor in some unspecified way — completely delusional
jokes.explanation: A good Michael self-delusion beat — the implication that Michael was banned from the birth because of his humor and then somehow 'proved him wrong' is characteristically delusional. The unspecified victories are funnier than any explanation would be.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'I try to pick up and hold a baby every day, if possible, because it nourishes me. It feeds my soul. Babies are drawn to me, and I think it's because they see me as one of them. But cooler, and with my life put together a little bit.'
jokes.setup: Michael explains his philosophy about babies
jokes.punchline: 'But cooler, and with my life put together a little bit' — the qualifiers undercut everything and reveal Michael's complete lack of self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed Michael confessional. The escalating claim that babies see him as a peer is funny enough, but 'cooler, and with my life put together a little bit' is what makes it great — the tiny hedge acknowledges he's comparing himself to infants, which makes his self-assessment both sad and absurd.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'If a baby were president, there would be no taxes. There would be no war. There would be no government, and things could get terrible... It would be a better screenplay idea than a serious suggestion.'
jokes.setup: Michael is free-associating about babies and political philosophy
jokes.punchline: He talks himself into the problems of a baby presidency — 'things could get terrible' — then walks it back to 'probably better as a screenplay idea'
jokes.explanation: The mid-thought self-correction — Michael genuinely thinking through the consequences of baby-led anarchy and then pivoting to a screenplay pitch — is a great Michael moment. The earnest reconsideration is funnier than a pure absurdist statement would be.

jokes.text: Michael announces the baby as 'As... Trid. Trid Levinson.' — mispronouncing/splitting the name
jokes.setup: Michael is doing a formal Lion King-style presentation of the baby to the office
jokes.punchline: He still can't say 'Astrid' correctly, splitting it into 'As... Trid'
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the name gag — diminishing returns but still functional. The running gag structure is clear.

jokes.text: Michael attempts a Lion King-style presentation of baby Astrid, lifting her up — the office shouts 'Michael!' and he's stopped before he goes too high
jokes.setup: Michael announces he's doing the Lion King presentation
jokes.punchline: He actually tries to Simba-lift a newborn, causing alarm — the physical commitment to the bit is the joke
jokes.explanation: A great visual gag — Michael's instinct to do a Lion King presentation with a real newborn is both characteristically oblivious and physically alarming. The crowd reaction adds to the comedy. Works well as a physical bit and as a character statement.

jokes.text: Holly tries to check in on Michael emotionally and he snaps: 'I'm fine, weirdo. Such an HR weirdo. Try not to suck all the air out of there when you walk in.'
jokes.setup: Michael has promised Jan to act cold toward Holly; Holly tries to connect with him
jokes.punchline: His cold persona comes out as bizarre rudeness — 'Try not to suck all the air out of there when you walk in' — which is mean but also reveals how much effort the pretense costs him
jokes.explanation: The cringe is in Michael's unconvincing attempt at cruelty — he's clearly overcompensating. The insult itself is odd enough to be funny ('suck all the air out') and the 'such an HR weirdo' implies he's reaching for something generic and cold.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'So we had games planned, but the baby ruins all of them.' Michael: 'The baby doesn't ruin anything, Kevin, okay? The baby multiplies the fun.'
jokes.setup: The party games were designed for a pregnant woman who was going to give birth imminently
jokes.punchline: Kevin's blunt 'the baby ruins all of them' vs. Michael's furious denial that 'the baby multiplies the fun' — followed by 'Who wants to guess when the baby will be born?'
jokes.explanation: Kevin's literal truth-telling vs. Michael's defensive positivity is a reliable dynamic. 'The baby multiplies the fun' is a good Michael-ism. The follow-up 'Who wants to guess when the baby will be born?' (when she's already been born) is the best beat of the exchange.

jokes.text: The office hosts the baby shower guessing game 'when will the baby be born?' — the baby has already been born and is in the room
jokes.setup: Baby shower games were planned for a pregnant Jan
jokes.punchline: They play 'guess when the baby will be born' with a baby already present at the party
jokes.explanation: A solid situational irony joke — the game is immediately obsolete, which no one seems to notice or care about. The absurdity of proceeding anyway says everything about how these office parties work.

jokes.text: Jan dismisses the gift stroller: 'She already has a stroller. And this is way worse than the stroller she came with. She's got an Orbit. That's a $1,200 stroller.'
jokes.setup: The office proudly presents their chipped-in gift stroller
jokes.punchline: Jan immediately compares it unfavorably to her $1,200 Orbit stroller — with no social awareness that this is rude
jokes.explanation: Classic Jan cringe — her inability to receive a gift graciously while announcing the specific dollar amount of her superior stroller. 'That's a $1,200 stroller' delivered flatly is the punch. Good character integration for Jan's particular flavor of obliviousness.

jokes.text: Dwight: '$1,200 is what I spent on my whole bomb shelter.'
jokes.setup: The office is reacting to Jan revealing the stroller cost $1,200
jokes.punchline: Dwight contextualizes the cost by comparison to his bomb shelter budget
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Dwight one-liner. Eight words reveal an entire aspect of Dwight's character — he has a bomb shelter, he built it frugally, and he considers it a reasonable point of price comparison. The economy is exceptional and the character integration is about as high as it gets. This is a great example of The Office's efficient character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'For that kind of money, this stroller should be indestructible.'
jokes.setup: Still reacting to the $1,200 stroller revelation
jokes.punchline: Dwight's survivalist framing — a stroller should be 'indestructible' — reveals his tactical worldview applied to baby equipment
jokes.explanation: A good follow-up to the bomb shelter line, but diminishing returns — the joke is the same character note played again. 'Indestructible' is a good word choice that fits Dwight's survivalist worldview.

jokes.text: Jan sings 'Son of a Preacher Man' at the baby shower — she has been singing for 20 minutes
jokes.setup: Jan spontaneously begins singing at her own baby shower
jokes.punchline: Jim describes on the phone that everyone is just staring at her — she has been singing for 20 minutes — and the song is specifically about losing one's virginity next to a church
jokes.explanation: Jan singing at her own shower is a great character beat — it's humiliating for the room and completely consistent with Jan's narcissism and need for performance. The specific detail that the song is about losing one's virginity (relayed secondhand by Jim) adds a layer of inappropriate content that makes it better. The 20-minute duration is the kicker.

jokes.text: Jan singing 'Son of a Preacher Man' at the baby shower, alone, for 20+ minutes while the office stares
jokes.setup: Jim calls Pam to report on the baby shower
jokes.punchline: Jan is performing 'Son of a Preacher Man' — a song explicitly about losing your virginity — at her own baby shower, unaccompanied, for an extended period, while coworkers stare silently
jokes.explanation: The cringe horror of this scene is maximized by Jim's commentary to Pam — he's both witness and narrator. Jan choosing a song about losing virginity for a baby shower is inspired character-writing: she's utterly self-unaware about how it reads, and she commits to a 20-minute performance. The extended duration is itself the joke. Very strong character integration — this is Jan at her most gloriously oblivious.

jokes.text: Pam, on the phone from a laundromat, discovers she washed her lipstick: 'Great, I washed my lipstick.'
jokes.setup: Pam is doing laundry for the first time in a month at a laundromat — her solo life at art school
jokes.punchline: She washed her lipstick — a small mundane disaster that speaks to her adjustment struggles
jokes.explanation: A small, gentle joke — the washed lipstick is a sad-funny detail of Pam's slightly chaotic solo living. Not a standout moment but contributes to the episode's emotional texture.

jokes.text: Jan's baby is let outside and nearly goes near a fence/barbed wire; Jan shouts 'Don't hit the fence!' and 'Don't get stuck on the barbed wire!' and 'Playtime is over!'
jokes.setup: Baby Astrid is apparently outside (perhaps in her stroller or being held outside)
jokes.punchline: Jan is shouting warnings about barbed wire at a newborn infant — 'Playtime is over!' implies the newborn was having playtime
jokes.explanation: An absurdist scene where Jan treats a newborn like a toddler running around. 'Playtime is over!' is the funniest line — the implication that a newborn was having structured playtime. Slightly unclear from the transcript alone but contextually funny.

jokes.text: Creed: 'Must be like the tide at Omaha Beach.' (about the afterbirth floating in the tub birth)
jokes.setup: Jan is describing her tub birth: 'the afterbirth floats'
jokes.punchline: Creed's WWII beach landing comparison to afterbirth floating in a tub — delivered with complete deadpan
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Perfect Creed — maximum dark wit in minimum words. The Omaha Beach reference is unexpected, historically specific, viscerally vivid, and only Creed would make this connection. It's simultaneously the most apt and most disturbing metaphor for the situation. The fact that Jan has to defend her birth choice in response ('It's actually really hygienic') makes it funnier. Nine words that do extraordinary work. Comparable to the anchor examples for craft quality.

jokes.text: Jan: 'No, it's actually really hygienic, Creed. After the birth, you get out—' Creed: 'I'm done.'
jokes.setup: Jan attempts to defend the hygiene of tub births after Creed's Omaha Beach remark
jokes.punchline: Creed immediately opts out of the conversation the moment it turns clinical — 'I'm done' — showing he was only in for the dark joke
jokes.explanation: An exceptional button to the Creed Omaha Beach joke. 'I'm done' when Jan begins explaining the hygiene is character perfection — Creed made his dark observation and has no interest in the actual information. The economy of two words doing that much character work is remarkable. This and the preceding joke form the episode's best comedic one-two punch.

jokes.text: Michael says he should have been there to witness the birth: 'I could have helped.'
jokes.setup: Michael is upset he missed the birth — Jan gently explains why he wasn't there
jokes.punchline: 'I could have helped' — Michael sincerely believes he would have been a net positive at a tub birth he was banned from by the instructor
jokes.explanation: A small irony beat — Michael's certainty that he would have 'helped' at a birth he was specifically excluded from. Functional but not a standout.

jokes.text: Jan asks Michael to remind her to talk to him about Astrid's 529, then: 'Wake me in 20.'
jokes.setup: Jan has just shared an emotionally significant moment with Michael holding the baby
jokes.punchline: She immediately pivots to retirement planning ('529') and taking a 20-minute nap — the domestic pragmatism undercuts any sentimentality
jokes.explanation: Jan's efficient multi-tasking of college savings discussion and power napping in the middle of a baby shower is a good character joke. The 529 reference is specific and funny — Jan's controlling financial planning applied to a newborn.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'I usually love babies, but when I held Astrid I just felt... Shortchanged.'
jokes.setup: Michael reflecting on the emotional experience of holding Jan's baby
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'Shortchanged' — the word is both honest and reveals Michael's self-centeredness even in a moment meant to be about the baby
jokes.explanation: A beautifully calibrated Michael moment — the pause before 'Shortchanged' does a lot of work. The word is surprising (you'd expect 'sad' or 'confused') and reveals Michael's narcissism: his main feeling about holding a baby is that he personally got a bad deal. High economy, great structure, and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael approaches Darryl calling himself a 'baby-daddy' and asking for advice 'from one baby-daddy to another'
jokes.setup: Michael wants advice about not bonding with the baby
jokes.punchline: He approaches Darryl specifically as a fellow 'baby-daddy,' invoking the term with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The racial undertone to Michael's 'baby-daddy' usage is clear, and the scene knowingly addresses it. Setup for the better payoffs that follow. Michael's sincere use of the term is the initial joke.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'Hell, yeah. You know why? 'Cause that was my baby.' / Michael: 'You should stop calling yourself baby-daddy.' / Darryl: 'Because you're not a daddy, and it's not your baby.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks if Darryl immediately bonded with his baby
jokes.punchline: Darryl explains the bond came from the baby being his actual child — a simple truth that devastates Michael's premise — then directly tells him to stop calling himself baby-daddy
jokes.explanation: Darryl as Michael's blunt reality-checker is a great dynamic. 'Hell, yeah. You know why? 'Cause that was my baby' is a perfect deadpan deflation. Darryl's refusal to play along with Michael's self-narrative is always good, and this exchange is a clean example.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Why, Darryl? Because I'm quote white unquote, unquote?'
jokes.setup: Darryl tells Michael to stop calling himself baby-daddy
jokes.punchline: Michael assumes the objection is racial — 'because I'm quote white unquote, unquote?' — the double 'unquote' reveals his confusion with air-quote grammar
jokes.explanation: A standout Michael Scott line. The double 'unquote' is a brilliant grammatical error that reveals Michael learned air quotes by imitation and doesn't understand the structure. Combined with his immediate assumption that race is the issue (when Darryl's objection is completely logical), this line does multiple comedy layers at once. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Michael points to the watermelon: 'You feel connected to this?' Darryl: 'That's not a baby.' Michael: 'You want to hold me, see how you feel?' Darryl: 'Could I? No.'
jokes.setup: Darryl is cutting through Michael's rationalizations
jokes.punchline: Michael offers himself as a baby-substitute for Darryl to hold — 'You want to hold me, see how you feel?' — and Darryl's 'Could I? No.' is a brief moment of genuine temptation before refusal
jokes.explanation: The brief hesitation in 'Could I?' before Darryl's 'No' is perfect — it implies that on some level the offer is tempting, which is somehow more absurd than a flat refusal. Michael's sincere offer to be held is a great absurdist beat. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Michael points to the watermelon on Darryl's desk: 'You feel connected to this?' Darryl: 'That's not a baby.' Michael: 'You want to hold me, see how you feel?' Darryl: 'Could I?' Michael: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to explain why he didn't bond with Astrid — using his watermelon prop for comparison
jokes.punchline: Michael offers to let Darryl hold HIM to test the bonding theory. Darryl's surprised 'Could I?' followed by Michael's immediate 'No.' — a reversal of the setup
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed exchange. Michael offering to be held to test the bonding theory is wonderfully absurd. But the real joke is Darryl's 'Could I?' — he seems genuinely interested, which is both funny (Darryl wants to hold Michael?) and suggests a warmth beneath his gruffness. Michael's panicked 'No.' closes the loop perfectly. One of the episode's funniest exchanges.

jokes.text: Michael asks where Astrid is; someone says she's 'on a sales call.' Michael: 'On a what?' Response: 'Wah, more paper. Wah.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks where the baby is
jokes.punchline: Someone jokes she's on a sales call — then mimics a baby ordering paper: 'Wah, more paper. Wah.'
jokes.explanation: A fun small gag — the baby being imagined as an office worker on a sales call. 'Wah, more paper. Wah.' is a good execution of the joke, translating a baby cry into a paper order.

jokes.text: Michael: 'No, she's just on her coffee break. That's funny.' Then: 'She's with Angela.'
jokes.setup: The office is joking about baby Astrid working
jokes.punchline: Michael says 'that's funny' — narrating the humor rather than laughing — then reveals the mundane truth: she's with Angela
jokes.explanation: Michael announcing that something is funny rather than laughing is a recurring bit. Mild here. The 'She's with Angela' deflation is a small character note.

jokes.text: Michael tries to get baby Astrid to look at his finger for a photo — Angela gets involved — Michael: 'You don't flash around a newborn baby. Don't you know that?'
jokes.setup: Michael and Angela are both fussing over the baby trying to get a photo
jokes.punchline: Michael lectures Angela about camera flash and newborns — with all the authority of someone who has done absolutely none of the preparation Jan has
jokes.explanation: Michael asserting baby expertise he doesn't have is a recurring character note. Functional but not distinguished. The conflict with Angela adds mild cringe interest.

jokes.text: Michael's internal debate about telling Holly about her hygiene — 'She smells like old tomatoes and dirt.'
jokes.setup: Michael is being pulled away from something he wants to do and rationalizes it as a kindness toward Holly
jokes.punchline: His assessment that Holly smells like 'old tomatoes and dirt' — presumably false, given his attraction to her — delivered as genuine concern
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'old tomatoes and dirt' is what makes this work — it's an oddly specific insult that reveals Michael is making things up to maintain the cold act. The absurd detail is funny.

jokes.text: Dwight performs the 'bumper test' on the gift stroller — a prolonged sequence of slamming it into things to test its durability
jokes.setup: Dwight expressed concern that the stroller wasn't 'indestructible' for its price
jokes.punchline: He conducts a formal destructive test — the 'bumper test' — slamming the stroller repeatedly into walls/furniture
jokes.explanation: A well-executed physical callback — Dwight actually follows through on his concern about stroller durability with a 'bumper test.' The commitment to a named, formal testing procedure is perfectly Dwight. Good visual comedy that pays off earlier setup. The extended duration of the test adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: Jan asks where the stroller she came in with is — Dwight immediately says he put it in her trunk. The gift stroller he just destroyed is gone.
jokes.setup: Jan wants to leave with her $1,200 Orbit stroller
jokes.punchline: Dwight proactively moved Jan's stroller — revealing that he swapped the tested/destroyed stroller away and handled logistics with characteristic efficiency
jokes.explanation: A clean callback — Dwight's efficiency in moving the good stroller implies some awareness of what happened to the gift stroller. The moment is quick but satisfying as a structural close to the stroller subplot.

jokes.text: Jan asks Michael not to date Holly — Michael: 'That's... I hate her.' — then immediately starts defending Holly before walking back 'not that it matters, 'cause I don't'
jokes.setup: Jan makes a surprise request: don't date Holly
jokes.punchline: Michael's immediate denial ('I hate her') followed by his involuntary defense of Holly reveals his true feelings — the cringe of watching him realize he's given himself away
jokes.explanation: A good character cringe moment — Michael's feelings for Holly are too strong to suppress even for Jan. The overprotested denial is a reliable comedy structure, and Michael's specific deflection ('I hate her') before recovering is well-played. Emotionally resonant and funny.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Not that it matters, 'cause I don't, but...' — trailing off while clearly meaning the opposite
jokes.setup: Michael is digging deeper into his denial about Holly
jokes.punchline: The incomplete sentence that trails into 'but...' — he can't finish the lie, which confirms everything
jokes.explanation: A functional extension of the previous joke. The trailing sentence is good character work but not a strong standalone joke — it needs the previous beat to land.

jokes.text: Michael, after Jan and baby leave, silently approaches Holly — long pause — then: 'You still going to be mean to me?'
jokes.setup: Michael was rude to Holly all episode per Jan's request — now Jan has left
jokes.punchline: Holly was clearly retaliating in kind and Michael, totally unaware of how his behavior caused this, asks if she's still going to be mean — as if her coldness were arbitrary
jokes.explanation: A well-earned payoff to the Holly subplot. The extended pause before the line implies awkward silence in which Michael is processing the situation. 'You still going to be mean to me?' shows he has no awareness that his rudeness caused her response — a perfect Michael Scott blind spot. The tone shifts from cringe to sweet quickly after, which is the episode's emotional landing.

jokes.text: Michael asks Holly out with a simple 'Want to go out?' Holly says 'Yes.' — then Michael's talking head: 'I didn't feel much when I held Astrid, but I got a good feeling from Holly.'
jokes.setup: The episode has been building the Jan/Michael/Holly triangle
jokes.punchline: Michael's talking head contrasts his emotional response to the baby ('shortchanged') with his response to Holly — and the kicker is comparing a baby to a potential girlfriend as emotional options on equal footing
jokes.explanation: A beautiful episode-closing joke that reframes everything. Michael treating Holly and Astrid as comparable emotional experiences ('didn't feel much from the baby / good feeling from Holly') is exactly the kind of sideways emotional logic that makes Michael Scott a great character. The callback to 'shortchanged' makes this land harder.

jokes.text: Holly says 'Yes' to going out with Michael — Michael's talking head: 'I didn't feel much when I held Astrid, but I got a good feeling from Holly.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been emotional about not bonding with Astrid
jokes.punchline: He resolves the emotional thread not with a revelation about the baby but about Holly — comparing his feelings for her against those for an infant
jokes.explanation: A good emotional-comedic button — Michael's way of expressing romantic feeling is to compare it to not bonding with a baby. The framing is absurd but also sweetly Michael. Good economy and a satisfying structural callback.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's dueling voicemails — each calls the other, gets voicemail, leaves a message. Jim talks to Pam's outgoing message; Pam talks to Jim's.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam have been slightly out of sync all episode due to distance
jokes.punchline: They literally cannot reach each other and end up talking to each other's voicemails — mutual near-miss that is bittersweet and slightly funny
jokes.explanation: The dueling voicemails are a structural joke about the Jim/Pam distance — they keep just missing each other. More poignant than funny, but the form has comedic irony built in.

jokes.text: Jim's voicemail to Pam: 'I figured I'd catch you walking to your car, but guess you must be out or something. I'll leave a message.' — immediately after getting voicemail
jokes.setup: Jim calls Pam; gets her voicemail
jokes.punchline: His narration of what he thought would happen ('catch you walking to your car') and his placeholder observation ('I'll leave a message') while leaving a message — he narrates the act he's currently doing
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'I'll leave a message' — while leaving a message — is a small, relatable observational beat. It shows him slightly flustered, which is unusual and endearing. The voicemail sequence overall does emotional work but this specific beat is the comedic highlight.

jokes.text: Jim's voicemail message to Pam references 'that crazy guy who pushed you' at the laundromat — then remembers they went shopping the next day to buy a washer-dryer — 'And yet, here you are, back in a Laundromat.'
jokes.setup: Jim is leaving a long, rambling voicemail trying to connect with Pam
jokes.punchline: He tells the story of a laundromat attack that led to buying a washer-dryer — the implicit point being: why did they buy a washer-dryer if she's at a laundromat again?
jokes.explanation: A mild joke about Jim noticing the irony of a laundromat purchase not preventing laundromat visits. Works emotionally as a glimpse of their shared history but isn't particularly sharp as comedy.

jokes.text: Jim's voicemail: 'I'm headed home.' Then catches himself: 'I'm headed to my dorm. Not home.'
jokes.setup: Jim is wrapping up his voicemail to Pam, who is away at art school
jokes.punchline: He almost calls her dorm 'home' before catching himself — the slip reveals that wherever Pam is IS home for Jim
jokes.explanation: Bittersweet character comedy — the self-correction 'I'm headed to my dorm. Not home.' is both funny (the correction) and emotionally resonant (what it implies about Jim's feelings). A clean, economical moment.

tmdb_overview: Michael practices for the birth of Jan's baby by having Dwight go over possible birthing scenarios. Meanwhile, Michael tells Holly that he will pretend to dislike her for Jan's benefit.
